origin: North America; a red-fleshed crabapple traced to the 1800s, listed variously as Red Vein, Redvein, or Red Vein Crab. No breeder or introduction record survives.
harvest_window: Late season; late September into October in the maritime PNW
disease_notes: Nursery sources claim good general disease resistance and strong cold hardiness, but there is no extension or trial data behind this. Treat scab resistance as unverified in a wet maritime site.
description: A small red-fleshed crabapple with deep cranberry skin, dark red flesh and a sharply tangy, mildly astringent juice, used to add acid, color and some structure to blends — small additions push finished cider toward a rosé hue. Trees are small (12-16 ft mature), precocious at 2-4 years, and midseason blooming, so they need another midseason variety as a pollinizer. This is the weakest-documented entry in the set: no WSU, Cornell or other university trial data exists for it.
discrepancies: Absent from the WSU cultivar database (77 cultivars) and from all extension sources — every attribute here rests on nursery and produce-catalog copy, which is the bottom of the preference order. Sources also disagree on tree size: Trees of Antiquity calls it a very small tree at 12-16 ft, while crabapples of this class are commonly vigorous. Recorded vigor as weak per the only source that addresses it, and tannin as medium inferred from described astringency rather than measured. Name is ambiguous (Red Vein vs Redvein) with no accession standard, so the orchard's trees cannot be confirmed against any reference. Confidence held at low-medium for this reason.

origin: France — Normandy. Properly Cimetière de Blangy, from a tree in the cemetery at Blangy-le-Château, about 15 km north of Lisieux, in the Calvados / Pays d'Auge region. Approved for planting in Calvados in the 1949 and 1958 lists and retired from the official list in 1966.
harvest_window: Late season; late October into November
disease_notes: No documented resistance or susceptibility ratings in any source consulted. Treat scab, mildew and fireblight behavior as unknown for a maritime PNW planting and scout accordingly.
description: A French douce-amère (bittersweet) cider apple, medium-sized, round to round-conic, green with a red sun flush. Long Ashton analysis lists it as a late bittersweet at 0.16% malic acid and 0.28% tannin — very low acid with soft, moderate tannin, making it a body-and-mouthfeel component rather than a structural one. It flowers in mid cider-apple season and is self-sterile, overlapping well with Improved Foxwhelp; synonyms include Blangy, Blagny, Cimetiere du Pays and Cimitiere.
discrepancies: Two independent sources agree on chemistry: Long Ashton lists Cimetiere as a late bittersweet at 0.16% malic acid / 0.28% tannin, and Pomiferous independently reports 0.16% malic acid — good corroboration. Not present in the WSU database, so no maritime-Washington harvest or bloom data exists and the late-October window is transposed from Normandy and Long Ashton. Main unresolved issue is identity: the orchard's label Cimetere could correspond to Cimetière de Blangy or to another Cimetière selection, and Long Ashton lists only the bare name Cimetiere without qualifier. Recorded the Blangy attribution because it is the only Cimetière with a documented cider record, but this should be confirmed against the nursery invoice.

origin: England — Somerset, associated with the Lambrook / South Petherton area. The clone sold commercially is Improved Lambrook Pippin. No raiser or introduction date is recorded.
harvest_window: Late mid-season; through October, still pressable in early November
disease_notes: No published disease ratings found in any source.
description: A Somerset sharp cider apple and heavy cropper, valued for supplying acidity to blends dominated by low-acid bittersweets. The juice is described as mild-sharp with good sugar content, and the fruit is crisp and juicy enough to eat fresh in October. Makes a vigorous, spreading tree.
discrepancies: Cross-check failed to produce a second substantive source. Absent from the WSU database, absent from the Long Ashton compositional tables, and absent from Orange Pippin — the only real source is one UK nursery listing, with a cider blog confirming the variety exists and has been pressed as a vintage single-varietal. No bloom group, SG, tannin or disease data exists anywhere, so those are recorded null or as sharp-class defaults rather than guessed. Also worth flagging a naming trap: Lambrook Pippin is unrelated to Dabinett despite Dabinett having been found at Middle Lambrook, South Petherton — same locality, different variety. Confidence is low and should stay low until the owner can supply nursery provenance.

origin: New Zealand — chance seedling found in 1952 by O. Moran at Waiwhero in the Moutere Hills near Motueka; 2020 parentage work identifies it as Delicious x Sturmer Pippin, with Lady Hamilton as a sibling.
harvest_window: Late; mid-to-late October in the PNW, stores until spring. In western Washington full maturity is not reliable every year.
disease_notes: Susceptible to apple scab, powdery mildew and rust, and somewhat susceptible to fireblight. Prone to internal (Braeburn) browning in storage. Scab pressure is the main practical concern on the Olympic Peninsula and it will need a spray program that the scab-immune varieties in this planting do not.
description: A late, crisp, high-acid commercial dessert apple, partially self-fertile but cropping better with a mid-to-late bloom partner such as Fuji or Granny Smith. In cider it contributes acid and aromatics rather than sugar or tannin — cidermakers report roughly 71% juice yield at about pH 3.2 and 11 Brix — so it functions as a sharp aromatic base rather than a standalone. Needs thinning to avoid alternate bearing.
discrepancies: Not in the WSU cider cultivar database — it is a commercial dessert cultivar, evaluated by WSU tree fruit programs rather than the Mount Vernon cider trial — so no maritime-Washington cider juice data is available and the SG/Brix figures come from cidermaker reports rather than trial analysis. Harvest timing conflicts by region: New Zealand and general references say mid-October, but Braeburn is a very late-maturing cultivar bred for a warmer, sunnier climate, and on the Olympic Peninsula it frequently runs into autumn rain before reaching full sugar. Recommended keeping the mid-to-late October window but flagging the maturity risk explicitly, since that is the site-specific fact the general sources omit. Ploidy is well established as diploid across references and is not in dispute.

origin: USA — grown from seed by nurseryman A.R. Whitney at Whitney Nursery, Franklin Grove, Illinois, around 1865; first recorded 1869.
harvest_window: Early to early-mid season; August into early September in the PNW
disease_notes: Reported as having good general disease resistance and exceptional cold hardiness; Montana State historically recommended it as a top crabapple for the state. No specific scab or fireblight ratings from any trial.
description: A large crabapple at 1-2 inches — well above typical crab size — greenish-yellow with red blush and stripes, with juicy crisp flesh and a sweet-sharp, mildly astringent flavor. Genuinely multipurpose for fresh eating, sauce, jelly and cider, and reported at about 11.4% sugar, enough to ferment past 5% ABV. Bears heavy crops young and is best blended with other early-season fruit, particularly bittersweets, since it ripens well ahead of the bittersweets in this planting.
discrepancies: Origin, date and fruit description corroborate cleanly across Montana State Extension and multiple nurseries. Not in the WSU database — the only crab evaluated there is Virginia Crab (Hewes) — so there is no maritime-WA juice analysis, and the 11.4% sugar figure comes from a nursery rather than a trial. Sources disagree on how much this is a cider apple at all: Montana State and most nurseries frame it as a dessert/culinary crab with cider as a secondary use, while cider-specific listings emphasize the fermentation potential. Recorded it as a crab with medium rather than high tannin, following the fresh-eating descriptions, because nothing measured supports a high-tannin claim. Ploidy set to unknown — no source states it, and inferring diploid from its use as a pollinizer would be a guess.

origin: France — properly Amère de Berthecourt, raised from a pippin at Parisis Fontain in Berthecourt (Oise/Normandy) in the 1850s. The name means the bitter apple from Berthecourt.
harvest_window: Mid to late season; October into early November
disease_notes: Somewhat susceptible to scab, powdery mildew and canker, and specifically sensitive to fireblight during bloom. That bloom-time fireblight sensitivity is the key planting decision here: pair it with a fireblight-resistant rootstock (G.890 or G.935) rather than MM.106.
description: A classic French bittersweet with small oblate yellow fruit flushed pink, unsuitable for eating. It presses to a rich amber juice with honeyed sugar, notes of vanilla and grass, and a long bitter finish, so it is used to add body and tannin to both hard and sweet cider. Prolific and easy to grow with a vigorous, spreading habit.
discrepancies: Origin story, bittersweet class and fireblight sensitivity agree across four independent nurseries including Cummins. Not in the WSU database, and notably it appears on cider.org.uk only in the Geneva, NY table rather than the Long Ashton table — meaning the North American compositional record derives from the USDA Geneva repository, the same collection that produced the documented Tremlett's Bitter mislabel. Recommend treating US-sourced Amere de Berthcourt provenance as unverified until fruit characters are checked against French descriptions (small, oblate, yellow with pink blush). No source gives SG or a bloom group; bloom group 4 is inferred from French bittersweets generally being late-blooming plus the reported bloom-time fireblight exposure, so it is the weakest field in this record.

origin: England — raised in the 19th century at Yarlington, Somerset, by nurseryman Harry Masters of Woolston. Despite the Jersey name it is Somerset, not Channel Islands, in origin; also known as Port Wine.
harvest_window: Early-to-mid October in maritime western Washington (WSU Mount Vernon mean harvest 10/9); late October to early November in England
typical_sg: 1.051 (WSU Mount Vernon, 12.5 Brix); 1.056 in English Long Ashton data
disease_notes: Susceptible to scab and fireblight per UK and US nursery sources; one source rates it only slightly scab-susceptible but resistant to brown rot. No scab or fireblight rating is published in the WSU trial data, so susceptibility should be assumed under Olympic Peninsula scab pressure.
description: A well-regarded vintage-quality bittersweet with medium conical fruit heavily flushed dark red and hard, dry white flesh. WSU Mount Vernon measured it at SG 1.051, 12.5 Brix, 0.19% malic acid, 0.21% tannin, pH 4.34, 174 mL/lb juice yield, with mean bloom 5/16 and harvest 10/9 — a genuine low-acid bittersweet, though less tannic in western Washington than English data suggests. WSU rates it productive (3.9/5) with high bloom density (4.1/5), semi-spur bearing and a spreading habit, and their tasters found it good enough to stand alone with a fruity aroma and melon, berry and butterscotch notes.
discrepancies: Two real conflicts, both resolved toward WSU. First, chemistry: Long Ashton (England) gives SG 1.056 / 0.32% tannin / 0.20% acid, while WSU Mount Vernon gives SG 1.051 / 0.21% tannin / 0.19% acid. Acid agrees closely but WSU measured barely two-thirds the tannin. Recommended the WSU figures as the planning numbers because they come from the same marine climate as this orchard — expect a softer, less tannic juice here than English literature implies, and blend accordingly. Second, tree habit: UK nurseries describe it as low-vigor, tip-bearing and strongly biennial needing careful pruning, whereas WSU records semi-spur bearing, spreading habit, only semi-alternate bearing and a solid 3.9/5 productivity. Recommended moderate vigor and moderate (not high) biennial tendency per WSU, while noting the tip-bearing claim is worth verifying on-site since it changes pruning strategy. Harvest date likewise pulled forward to early October on WSU data.

origin: England — raised in Devon in the late 19th century. Critically, most North American material is NOT this variety; see discrepancies.
harvest_window: Late September to mid-October. WSU Mount Vernon records mean harvest 9/30 for the US Geneva material; true English Tremlett's is early-to-mid October.
typical_sg: 1.044 for the US Geneva material at WSU Mount Vernon (10.9 Brix); the true English variety runs roughly 1.050-1.058
disease_notes: Frost resistant and generally hardy; no scab or fireblight ratings published by WSU or Long Ashton. WSU rated the Geneva material 2.0 for blind wood, indicating a meaningful tendency to bare branch sections that affects pruning.
description: The true English variety is a hard-tannin Devon bittersweet, yellow flushed and lightly striped red, with sweet-astringent flesh; Long Ashton lists it at 0.27% malic acid and 0.34% tannin, high enough to carry a medium-dry cider close to single-varietal. It crops well but is strongly biennial. Before relying on any of this, confirm which variety you actually have — the fields above describe the English original, but if these trees came from a US nursery they are most likely the mis-catalogued Geneva clone, which behaves as a sharp, not a bittersweet.
discrepancies: This is the most serious discrepancy in the set and it is an identity problem, not a measurement problem. WSU Mount Vernon lists the cultivar as Tremlett's (Geneva) and annotates it explicitly: Not the true Tremlett's Bitter. WSU classifies it as SHARP — tannin 0.17%, malic acid 1.01%, pH 3.17, SG 1.044, 10.9 Brix, harvest 9/30, bloom 5/5, alternate bearing yes, productivity only 2.8/5. Long Ashton's true English Tremlett's Bitter is a BITTERSWEET at 0.34% tannin and 0.27% acid. These are opposite ends of the classification system: roughly four times the acid and half the tannin. The cause is a mis-catalogued tree at the USDA Geneva, NY repository from which most US nurseries propagated. Recommendation: if these trees were bought from a North American nursery, assume the Geneva clone and use the WSU numbers — a low-sugar, very high-acid sharp that will acidify a blend rather than add tannin, and a weak cropper at 2.8/5 productivity. The cider_type, acidity, tannin and SG fields above describe the English original as requested by the variety name, but they are probably wrong for the actual trees. Resolve by measuring juice pH at harvest: below about 3.3 confirms the Geneva clone, above about 4.0 confirms the true bittersweet.

origin: England — found by William Dabinett as a wilding in a hedge at Middle Lambrook, South Petherton, Somerset, in the mid-19th century; probably a seedling of Chisel Jersey. Correct spelling is Dabinett; Dabinette is the orchard's own label.
harvest_window: Mid-October in maritime western Washington (WSU Mount Vernon mean harvest 10/14); late October into November in England
disease_notes: No standout resistance; treat as ordinary susceptibility for scab and canker in a wet climate. Late flowering (WSU mean bloom 5/19, the latest of the WSU-recorded varieties in this planting) gives useful spring frost avoidance.
description: The benchmark English bittersweet and one of the most planted cider varieties in Somerset, with small yellow-green fruit flecked red. WSU Mount Vernon measured SG 1.055, 13.5 Brix, 0.22% malic acid, 0.24% tannin, pH 4.41 and an excellent 242 mL/lb juice yield, with productivity 3.7/5, semi-spur bearing, spreading habit and semi-alternate bearing. It is self-fertile and flowers late, and is one of the few varieties that can stand as a single-varietal cider — though see the sensory caveat below.
discrepancies: Chemistry agrees well between WSU Mount Vernon (SG 1.055, 0.22% acid, 0.24% tannin) and Long Ashton (SG 1.055-1.057, 0.18% acid, 0.29% tannin) — the closest agreement of any variety in this set, so confidence is high. Two smaller conflicts. Harvest: English sources say late October into November, WSU records 10/14 — used the WSU date for local planning. Sensory is the interesting one: English literature almost universally describes Dabinett's tannin as soft, well-integrated and well-balanced, whereas WSU's professional taster panel found tannins are harsh and tend to dominate flavor and recommended it as a blender for those not wanting a robust single-varietal. Recommended flagging both readings rather than picking one, since the WSU panel tasted fruit grown in this climate but the English view reflects far more cidermaking history. Practical read: do not assume a soft single-varietal here without trialing it.

origin: Russia — first noted around 1826 near Kursk, western Russia, probably as a wild seedling. Antonovka is a group of related cultivars rather than one clone; Common Antonovka (Antonovka Obyknovennaya) is the widespread member.
harvest_window: Late fall to early winter; harvest can begin mid-September and runs into October
disease_notes: Reported scab resistant, drought tolerant and exceptionally cold hardy — seedling rootstocks are rated to about -45C, USDA zone 3. Slow to come into bearing, then crops heavily. Cold hardiness is largely irrelevant at this site; the scab resistance is the useful trait on the Olympic Peninsula, though it is not backed by trial data.
description: A major Eastern European culinary apple with pure white, aromatic, strongly acidic flesh that sweetens only when fully ripe, used for cooking and juice as much as fresh eating, and useful as a high-acid blending component. It is better known outside Russia as a seedling rootstock, producing vigorous, deep-taprooted, well-anchored, standard-sized, very cold-hardy trees. Flowering group 3 and not self-fertile, so it needs a pollination partner.
discrepancies: Not in the WSU database, so no maritime-WA data. The substantive problem is that Antonovka is a cultivar group, not a single variety, which makes several widely repeated claims unreliable. Ploidy: changed from diploid to unknown on cross-check — Common Antonovka is generally treated as diploid, but the group includes Antonovka ploskaya, a tetraploid used in breeding, so the label alone does not fix ploidy. The comes true from seed claim is repeated by nearly every nursery but is horticultural shorthand for unusually uniform seedlings, not genetic truth; seedlings vary. Second ambiguity, and the one that matters for the orchard record: Antonovka is sold both as a scion cultivar and as a seedling rootstock, so an entry labeled Antonovka may describe either. Recommend the owner confirm whether these are grafted Antonovka scions or Antonovka-rooted trees of another variety before the record is trusted.

origin: True Puget Spice is a WSU Mount Vernon release (2012) from a Prima x Alkmene cross — standard apple parents, classed as a crab on fruit size only. These orchard trees were sold as Puget Spice but are believed mislabeled, so the actual identity of the trees on site is unknown.
harvest_window: Mid-October for true Puget Spice (WSU Mount Vernon mean harvest 10/15). The actual trees' window must be confirmed by observation.
disease_notes: True Puget Spice is scab immune and mildew resistant — its main selling point for maritime western Washington, and the single easiest diagnostic here. If these trees show scab, that is direct evidence of the mislabel.
description: Recorded as Fake Puget Spice because the orchard's trees were purchased as Puget Spice but are believed mislabeled — every attribute below describes what Puget Spice should be, not necessarily what is growing. True Puget Spice is a small (1.70 inch) WSU-bred cider crab that its breeder classifies as BITTERSHARP: WSU measured tannin 0.13%, malic acid 0.96%, pH 3.28, SG 1.057, 13.5 Brix, with a perfect 5/5 bloom density and 5/5 productivity, upright habit, standard bearing and no alternate bearing. WSU tasters describe high acidity and high astringency, straw colored, a great blender providing mouthfeel. It blooms very early (mean 4/25, the earliest in this planting) and needs a pollinizer.
discrepancies: Nursery copy is substantially wrong about this variety and WSU — the breeding program that released it — contradicts it directly. Nurseries describe Puget Spice as high in tannic acid with a juice profile similar to Kingston Black, usable as a single-varietal. WSU's own data shows tannin at just 0.13%, which is BELOW WSU's own 0.2% threshold for the bitter classes; the fruit is bittersharp because of very high acid (0.96% malic, pH 3.28), not because of tannin. Recommended tannin as low and acidity as high on WSU data, and reframed its blending role as acid and astringent mouthfeel rather than tannin. Second conflict: Raintree says early season ripening in September, WSU records mean harvest 10/15 — used the WSU date. Third: Raintree calls it bloom group 2 while WSU's mean bloom date of 4/25 is the earliest of any variety here, consistent with group 1-2; kept 2. All of this describes the true variety, which these trees probably are not, so treat the whole record as a reference target for identification rather than as a description of the orchard's fruit.
